slides.title: Visualization As A Design Pipeline
slides.notes: Open by defining visualization as a graphics discipline for human judgment. The important contrast is not static versus interactive, but whether a person must compare, explore, explain, or decide. Preview the pipeline from data abstraction through validation so every later technique has a purpose.

slides.title: Why Visualization Is Needed
slides.notes: Use this slide to name the three scarce resources. Computation limits how much data can be processed, human attention limits how much can be inspected, and display capacity limits how much can be shown. Good visualization design balances all three instead of merely drawing more marks.

slides.title: Data Types Drive Encoding Choices
slides.notes: Before choosing a chart, classify the data. Quantitative, ordered, categorical, temporal, relational, and spatial fields support different operations and different visual channels. The notebook dataset is useful because one synthetic table contains all of these types and makes the classification concrete.

slides.title: Task Abstraction
slides.notes: Emphasize that domain questions become reusable abstract tasks. A facilities question about inspection becomes find outliers and locate them; a question about failures becomes follow graph paths. This abstraction step is what lets visualization knowledge transfer across scientific, engineering, and operational domains.

slides.title: Transform Data Before Drawing
slides.notes: The chapter warns against treating raw columns as automatically ready for display. Derived dimensions such as risk score, status, uncertainty, clusters, and principal components often expose the question more directly. The cost is that every transformation needs a recorded validation check.

slides.title: Marks And Channels
slides.notes: Present marks as geometric carriers and channels as the adjustable properties of those marks. Position is usually the most accurate channel for quantitative comparison, while hue works well for a small set of categories. The slide should make encoding choice feel like a resource allocation problem.

slides.title: Color Must Match The Data
slides.notes: Use the luminance strip to separate category color from ordered color. A sequential map gives a stable lightness order for risk or magnitude, while rainbow hue can reverse perceived order. The notebook check makes this measurable with zero sequential reversals and many rainbow reversals.

slides.title: Spatial Layout And Labels
slides.notes: Explain that spatial layout is either data given by the problem or a visual choice made by the designer. Two-dimensional layouts are easier to inspect than unnecessary 3D, and labels should be staged carefully because text is precise but consumes display and attention quickly.

slides.title: Interaction Changes The Question State
slides.notes: Interaction is not decoration; it changes the current data subset, viewport, ordering, or detail level. The canonical pattern is overview first, then zoom and filter, then details on demand. Ask students to identify exactly what state changes after each user action.

slides.title: Composition Coordinates Multiple Views
slides.notes: A single view is easiest to read when it is sufficient, but complex tasks often need layers, small multiples, or linked panels. The key invariant is consistency: the same selection, axes, categories, and encodings must mean the same thing across the composed views.

slides.title: Relational Data Needs Two Readings
slides.notes: Graphs are a good example of why composition matters. Node-link drawings support path following but can accumulate crossings, while adjacency matrices remove crossings and make dense structure easier to compare. Neither representation dominates; the right choice follows the task.

slides.title: Reduction Is A Declared Tradeoff
slides.notes: When there are too many items or dimensions, reduction becomes unavoidable. Aggregation, filtering, focus plus context, and dimensionality reduction each remove or reshape information. The instructor should ask what is preserved, what is discarded, and which invariant proves the reduction behaved correctly.

slides.title: Validation And Uncertainty
slides.notes: Validation happens at several layers, from the domain question to the algorithm and artifact files. Uncertainty should be visible when decisions depend on confidence. The notebook checks calibration, interval coverage, selection semantics, and artifact integrity so claims are backed by evidence.

slides.title: Visualization Examples
slides.notes: Use the examples as a taxonomy, not as a gallery. Tables, graphs, trees, maps, and spatial fields all combine data types, tasks, encodings, interaction, and reduction differently. The point is to recognize the design pattern behind the example rather than memorize one layout.

slides.title: Design Review Ledger
slides.notes: This slide turns the lecture into a working design review. Each row states a domain question, data type, abstract task, marks and channels, interaction, reduction, and validation. Students should be able to change one column and predict which downstream choices must change.

slides.title: Chapter Recap
slides.notes: Close by making the habit explicit. A visualization is a chain of accountable design decisions: name the data, name the task, choose channels, add interaction or composition only when needed, reduce deliberately, and validate both perception and computation before trusting the display.
